title: Double charges and refund races
idea: A double charge happens when two requests with one Idempotency-Key both see it as new; the fix claims the key atomically and updates refund totals with compare-and-set.

analogy.text: A ticket slot that fits one ticket. Two people push copies of the same ticket at once; the slot takes one, and the other bounces back.
analogy.breaks: A slot never times out; a PROCESSING payment must be reconciled.

points: Check-then-act on the key map lets two threads both charge.
`putIfAbsent` claims the key atomically; the loser sees PROCESSING and stops.
Refund totals use `compareAndSet`: re-read and retry when another refund wins.
A timeout stays PROCESSING; a reconciler asks the gateway for the truth.

steps.caption: Unsafe version. A double-click sends two requests with key k-1. Both ask whether k-1 is known.
The map is still empty, so both get no. Neither knows about the other.
A records k-1 and calls the gateway.
B acts on its stale no, overwrites the key and charges too. The customer pays twice.
Safe version. Both requests call `putIfAbsent` on k-1 at the same moment.
The map applies one call at a time for k-1. A's call writes PROCESSING and gets null back.
Only the call that got null goes on to charge.
B's call returns the existing PROCESSING value. B reports in progress and never charges.

code.title: Prove the double charge
code.caption: A barrier forces both requests to collide every run, so the race shows up deterministically.

walk.text: Run the same double-click race twice: unsafe, then with `putIfAbsent`.
Edge case: the charge times out, the retry is a replay, then reconcile settles it.
Two threads, one key, and a barrier; join both before reading the count.
Safe: only the call that gets null from `putIfAbsent` goes on to charge.
Unsafe: both check, wait for each other, then both claim and charge.
`pay` claims the key once. A timeout leaves PROCESSING, and replays return it.
`replace` swaps only from PROCESSING, so reconcile never overwrites a final status.

code.title: Refunds with compare-and-set
code.caption: Two agents refund 30000 each from a 50000 payment at the same moment.

walk.text: Start both agents, count accepted refunds, and return the refunded total.
Unsafe: read, wait, check, write. Both pass the check on a stale read.
CAS: write only if the total is still what you read; otherwise re-read.

pitfalls: Never check `containsKey` then `put`; claim the key with `putIfAbsent`.
Never call the gateway while holding a lock or inside a map update; I/O blocks others.
A request that finds PROCESSING must poll or wait, never charge again.

quiz.q: What is the first line RefundGuard prints?
options: It changes from run to run
quiz.why: The barrier makes both agents read 0 before checking. Both pass the 50000 limit check and both add 30000.

takeaway: Claim keys and refund totals atomically, and reconcile timeouts instead of guessing.

starters: Why does a ConcurrentHashMap not stop the first race?
What should the second request return while the first is PROCESSING?
How often should a reconciler poll the gateway?
